## belief

### A Boundary Will Drive Them Away
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Her precise diagnosis of why boundaries fail on this side: the problem is rarely not knowing where the line is, it is not being able to stand behind it. What the person most wants — closeness and co-regulation — sits on the far side of the boundary, so holding it feels like choosing against the thing itself.

### A Partner Will Make Me Feel Worthy
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The anxious premise underneath the stated wish for a long-term relationship: that another person will supply feeling protected, stable and worth loving. Once conflict starts, what is being defended is not the relationship but those feelings — which is why the argument stops tracking the thing it is nominally about.

### A Relationship Is A Checklist Item
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant premise: a life is designed first and a person is then sought who slots into it without requiring much change. In conflict what gets defended is the completeness of the arrangement and the self-image resting on it, rather than the relationship.

### An Apology Must Promise It Will Never Happen Again
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The assumption that a serious apology has to come with a guarantee, and that anything less will not save the relationship. Priebe's objection is that a pattern laid down in infancy does not end after one bad night and ten minutes of reflection, so the guarantee is usually a lie — and a lie repeated across several apologies is what actually costs you the person's trust.

  - healed_by → Apologising With An Action Plan (https://youtu.be/31aWIy9jp5I?t=560)
  - contrasts_with → Impact Regardless Of Intent (https://youtu.be/31aWIy9jp5I?t=520)
  - source: What To Do When You Mess Up (Attachment Healing) @480s — https://youtu.be/31aWIy9jp5I?t=480

### Any Criticism Means I Am Being Written Off
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

Feedback can only be taken in by someone who trusts they are being seen whole — and if nobody has been shown the whole of you, nobody can. So a single note reads as: none of this is wanted. Priebe describes a support group whose members had seen each other vulnerable before giving feedback, and the first time her body registered criticism as care rather than as being written off.

### Anything That Feels Bad Is Bad
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

A system that received comfort but not protection concludes that bad feeling is itself the problem. The cost is that genuinely protective moves — naming a limit, having the necessary conflict early — all feel bad in the moment and so get read as mistakes.

### Boundaries Are Barriers
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Reading a limit as a wall between two people rather than the thing that makes them visible to each other. It is why boundaries feel threatening on this side rather than merely inconvenient — the instinct is that every line drawn is closeness withheld.

### Communicating Pain Is Useless
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

She names this as the largest single obstacle in her own healing: the conviction that there is no point telling anyone what hurts. Her way out was narrow but sufficient — granting that nobody may understand your situation better than you do, while accepting that other people can still see the parts of it you cannot.

*belief · synthesis · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

### Everything That Happens Is My Doing
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Every child starts life assuming they are the cause of what happens around them. Most get that corrected by bringing their reading of events to someone older who can disconfirm it. Without co-regulation that correction never arrives, so the assumption survives into adulthood as a conviction that outcomes could not possibly have been shaped by anyone else.

### Feeling Things Means Losing Control
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The fear that keeps avoidant people out of the work, and she says it is close to universal among them: that attending to feeling means being permanently at its mercy. Her answer is that the causation runs the other way — a feeling you can see is one you have options about, and a repressed one acts on you unobserved.

### Good Intentions Mean I Cannot Have Caused Harm
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Priebe names this as a characteristic error of the anxious style: I meant well, therefore I did not do anything wrong, therefore if there is a problem it belongs to them — they are toxic, or a narcissist. The step that is missing is the ordinary one secure people make without strain: you can act on good intentions and still hurt someone, and the hurt is real either way.

### Having Boundaries Makes Me A Bad Person
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Learned in a family where needs were fused and personal limits were not permitted: in a relationship you may not have boundaries, and everything asked of you is owed, in exchange for love. Priebe notes the fearful-avoidant version has a release valve the anxious version lacks — outside a relationship, all of it is allowed again.

### I Am Innocent
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Her deepest layer, and the most uncomfortable. Where warmth and validation were genuinely owed and not given, a kind of childlike purity persists — a self-concept as endlessly giving, which has never had to absorb that good intentions still injure people. Intimacy requires setting that ego down, which is precisely why it is frightening.

### I Am Lovable In So Far As I Am Self-Sufficient
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant model of how love arrives: keep everything running well, and someone will turn up, admire the finished life, and that will be love. Priebe's correction is that secure love is two people seeing each other's difficulties and supporting each other through them — so a secure partner will come looking for where you struggle, which is precisely what the model has no place for.

### I Am Not Okay And Neither Are You
*belief · literature · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The fearful-avoidant position, and the exact inverse of the secure one. Where security holds that both parties are basically alright, this holds that neither is — so there is no stable place to stand, in another person or in oneself.

### I Am Okay, You Are Not Okay
*belief · literature · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant position. Having learned to self-regulate early and without much help, there can be some pride in the competence and considerable judgement toward people who lack it. She notes what gives the projection away: irritation at someone else's dysregulation only makes sense if it were somehow yours to manage.

### I Can Bear Anything
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

What follows from not registering the cost. If nothing quite lands as painful, no situation gets ruled out — so instead of leaving, you accept the circumstances and set about navigating them cleverly. She puts the correction plainly: being able to find a way through something difficult is not a reason to be in it.

### I Can Heal Without Changing Anything Else
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The assumption Priebe says attachment work rarely challenges: that you get healthier and your existing life improves around you. Her counter is that a life has usually been built out of situations the old strategy navigates well, and some of them — including sources of livelihood and of genuine connection — will not survive the change.

### I Can Protect Myself But Not Comfort Myself
*belief · synthesis · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant inverse. Behaving correctly heads off rejection, so protection is learnable — but if pain lands anyway you are alone with it. She notes this rarely presents as refusing help: reaching out simply never occurs to the person as an option.

### I Cannot Be Okay Until They Change
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

Her single test for whether you are in the triangle. The grievance may be entirely legitimate — someone may genuinely have wronged you — and it makes no difference: while your wellbeing waits on somebody else's move, it is not in your hands. She names this as the thing that has to go before attachment work can begin at all.

### I Intend To Die With These Parts Unseen
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Not a decision to be private but a standing plan that the shameful parts stay hidden permanently. Priebe contrasts it with the secure pattern, which also does not disclose everything immediately but does disclose progressively as trust accumulates. The plan is what makes intimacy something that can only happen by accident.

### I Lost Myself In That Relationship
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The central error she names, and the one that guarantees repetition. Seeing the suppressed half emerge under pressure, the conclusion drawn is that the partner produced it — so the next search is for someone who will not. Her correction is exact: nothing was lost in that relationship, something was found that is normally kept out of view.

The reading a child makes of intermittent success. If the same signal works sometimes and fails other times, the difference must lie in how clearly it was sent — so the answer is to send it louder. This is the premise underneath every escalation.

### I Will Only Be Happy Once You Meet My Needs
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The unconscious sentence running underneath anxious conflict, and the definition of the victim corner. It was learned honestly: press hard enough on what hurts and the caregiver came. Priebe notes the adult version pushes an avoidant partner away precisely because it works by crossing the boundary they are most defended around.

### I Would Contaminate A Healthy Person
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The anxious style doubts its desirability while holding that it is fundamentally well-meaning with a lot of love to give. The avoidant holds that it is solid and has plenty to offer practically. The fearful-avoidant, seeing its own strategic and manipulative moves clearly, concludes that it is bad — and so rejects the person offering healthy love, to protect them from it.

### I Would Not Be Compatible With Someone Healthier
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

A belief Priebe declines to simply refute. Stated as worth — nobody better would want me — it is false. Stated as skill — I do not yet have the equipment to relate to someone who communicates well — it is often accurate, and it names the actual work. The two readings feel identical from inside and lead to opposite conclusions.

### If I Feel Angry, I Must Be Being Irrational
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The conclusion a scapegoated child reaches, carried into adulthood as a standing veto on low-grade anger. Priebe describes spending most of her life certain she had an anger problem, and only later recognising that the problem ran the other way: the anger she felt at genuine injustices was never expressed, and only the overflow ever reached the surface.

### If It Does Not Make Sense I Am Not Feeling It
*belief · synthesis · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant bias: when a feeling has no defensible cause, the feeling is judged mistaken and reassigned to something else — too much coffee, not enough exercise. She points out this repeats the misattunement inward, telling yourself the thing happening in your body is not happening.

### If It Doesn't Hurt Me, It Doesn't Hurt Them
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The avoidant does not know their pain response is quieter than other people's, so their own reading becomes the reference. A partner in visible distress over something that would barely register is therefore performing, or angling for something. Priebe treats this as the honest source of a great deal of avoidant impatience — a calibration error, not contempt.

### If My Feeling Is Strong, Something Caused It
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Learned early and often accurate: a child in an unpredictable home whose feelings tracked what was going on around them. Carried into adulthood it becomes a rule — an intense feeling must have an external cause — with no room for a state that arose from somewhere else entirely and then went looking for something to attach to.

### If You Felt What I Feel, You Would Help Me
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Under activation the anxious system treats transmitting the feeling as the only route to relief: if the other person could be made to feel what I feel, they would give me the co-regulation that ends it. This makes accuracy about events negotiable — the story is instrumental, the feeling is the message.

*belief · synthesis · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Having formed its model of relationships around unpredictability, the system recognises unpredictability as the thing it is looking for. This is why the stated wish for a responsive partner and the actual pursuit so often point in opposite directions.

### Inside A Relationship I Cannot Have Boundaries
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Never having seen a boundary held inside an intimate relationship as a child, the adult concludes that partnership means total absorption — no asking for space, no asking for anything the other person does not already want. Which leaves exit as the only door to solitude, and makes every need for room look like a reason to leave.

*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The fear that keeps the box shut: that admitting the repressed half will mean being ruled by it. Her answer is that the opposite happens — what integration produces is discernment about which side to weight when, where the unintegrated version simply gets overtaken at unpredictable moments.

### Intimacy Will Cost Me My Stability
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The surface-level fear, and the reason avoidant people can look uncompromising from outside. It is rarely unwillingness to make room — it is that the scaffolding keeping them steady was built over decades without other people in it, and closeness threatens every piece of it at once.

*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The fearful-avoidant premise: deep connection with someone who sees only the vulnerabilities you have selected for them. The catch she names is that the material being withheld is the material intimacy is actually built from, so the premise rules out the thing it is asking for.

Learned where affection came in exchange for effort: that what you do, how you present, or what you can do for someone is the thing that makes you deserving. It produces overextension as a matter of course, since the alternative is not being owed anything.

The avoidant version of an impossible expectation, and the mirror of the anxious one. Where one demands that a relationship dissolve all insecurity, this demands a partner who never needs anything managed — and treats any lapse as evidence of the wrong person rather than of a person.

Her sharpest reading in this video: much of the anger anxious people direct at partners is, underneath, a complaint that the partner is not doing the boundary-setting on their behalf. *belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Strength read as self-sufficiency: needing nothing from anyone, never asking, handling it. Priebe separates appearing capable from being capable — the cost of the appearance is the perspective, feedback and complementary skill that only come from other people, plus the knowledge of what you do not know, which she treats as a component of competence rather than a concession.

### Once I Am Healed I Will Not Be Emotional
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Every style carries a slightly wrong picture of what recovery looks like, and this is the fearful-avoidant one: the emotions and needs that break through are read as the malfunction, so healing means stopping them. Priebe's counter runs the other way — the route out is making attachment needs more conscious day to day, not less, which is precisely what feels wrong.

### Only Someone With A History Like Mine Could Understand Me
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Priebe grants this one a great deal of ground. Fearful-avoidant lives often do not follow the ordinary sequence, and the coping machinery built around a complex history is genuinely hard for others to read — so finding someone who does understand is rare, and letting go of them is correspondingly hard. She calls that reasonable, and then notes what it costs when the rare person is also the wrong one.

### Pursue But Never Relax
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The instruction a child derives when the same person is both the source of care and the source of threat: you must pursue closeness because you need it to be alright, and you must never settle into it. It is the contradiction the entire fearful-avoidant pattern is built to execute.

*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The conclusion that follows from never bringing your own wants to a relationship: if you do not ask it for anything, it cannot give you anything, and the ledger will always read as loss.

A common fear on the anxious side, and she treats it as reasonable rather than silly. If the highs you know are the best feeling you have had, the prospect of losing them reads as loss — which is exactly why the fear is hard to argue someone out of from outside.

The conclusion drawn from repeated refusal. Not a judgement about emotion but a conditioned finding about what works: needs get met by appearing not to have any, or by having only the pleasant ones.

### Something Is Wrong With Me
*belief · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The deepest layer, and she says every insecure style holds some version of it. For avoidant patterning the shame attaches to having needs at all — without the accompanying knowledge that everyone has them and that secure people simply do not carry shame about it. Because a self-rejecting layer sits on top, someone else responding warmly is not enough to shift it.

The wager underneath limerence: that things become permanently alright if this particular person can be got to care in this particular way. It is why disconfirming evidence tends to raise the effort rather than lower it — the fantasy is doing a job, and losing it costs more than being wrong does.

The romantic form of the same premise: once a committed relationship is in place there will finally be someone permanently available to regulate you. She notes how much of our art and film encodes exactly this, which is part of why it goes so long unexamined.

### Vulnerability In A Partner Is Unattractive
*belief · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The fifth blindspot, and the most zoomed-out: which people you keep choosing. If the pattern is partners who present as sunny and unbothered, with the emotional availability expected to arrive later, it is worth asking whether availability is in fact a turn-off. Secure people show their feelings and expect the secure-base role to alternate — so the preference and the stated goal are pulling in opposite directions.

Learned where reaching out was reliably met with withdrawal or hostility. It is held as a bodily prediction rather than an opinion, which is why it keeps operating in people who would sincerely deny believing it.

## origin

### Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility
*origin · literature · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=feared fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The developmental condition behind avoidant patterning: reaching toward a caregiver in vulnerability or need predictably produced withdrawal or hostility rather than attunement. The lesson learned is not that people are bad, but that expressing need is what costs you them.

  - source: Avoidant Attachment: When Attraction Turns Off Without Warning (Unpacking Deactivation Triggers) @850s — https://youtu.be/7mElEzMpbeE?t=850
  - mirrors → Inconsistent Responsiveness (https://youtu.be/zv7ROoYCi6s?t=107)
  - source: How Does An Avoidant Attachment Style Develop? @107s — https://youtu.be/zv7ROoYCi6s?t=107
  - source: Attachment & Nervous System Wiring 101: How Childhood Shapes Your Thinking and Self-Regulation @1208s — https://youtu.be/sapNZnr9KYk?t=1208

### Frightening Caregiver
*origin · literature · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The condition in which the person who supplies everything you need to survive is also the source of danger. Her framing is that this need not be literal lethal threat — a caregiver who periodically loses control of themselves is, to an infant, an enormous animal in the room whose behaviour cannot be predicted, and the child has no coherent answer to whether approaching is safe.

  - mirrors → Inconsistent Responsiveness (https://youtu.be/_gCOo_vQM54?t=179)
  - source: How Does A Fearful-Avoidant Attachment Style Develop? @179s — https://youtu.be/_gCOo_vQM54?t=179

### Inconsistent Responsiveness
*origin · literature · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Care that arrived sometimes and not others. She is careful that this need not involve anything nameable as neglect — a parent with several children, an illness, exhausting work, or simply their own unprocessed material can produce it while trying hard. What the child registers is not cruelty but unpredictability.

  - mirrors → Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility (https://youtu.be/EdpaCMW1PHw?t=67)
  - source: How Does An Anxious Attachment Style Develop? @67s — https://youtu.be/EdpaCMW1PHw?t=67

### Intervention Only At Crisis Level
*origin · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

Care that arrived reliably but late — around seven to nine out of ten, by which point the child was already outside the window of tolerance. She draws a precise consequence: outside that window nobody absorbs the regulation being performed on them, so the soothing works in the moment and is never learned.

  - mirrors → Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility (https://youtu.be/sapNZnr9KYk?t=485)
  - part_of → The Distress Scale (https://youtu.be/sapNZnr9KYk?t=485)
  - source: Attachment & Nervous System Wiring 101: How Childhood Shapes Your Thinking and Self-Regulation @485s — https://youtu.be/sapNZnr9KYk?t=485

### Misattuned Mirroring
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

A caregiver who cannot tolerate a feeling in themselves reflects back something other than what the child is having — meeting sadness with insistent cheerfulness, well meant and inaccurate. Since children learn what they are feeling from how it is named for them, the result is lasting uncertainty about one's own internal states.

  - source: Learning Self-Regulation Through Self-Attunement @200s — https://youtu.be/TplLHhDRqAQ?t=200

### Over-Identification With The Child
*origin · priebe · anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

One of two failure modes she contrasts with sensitive parenting: the child's state read as a verdict on the parent. The distress then has to be pushed away, because the alternative is accepting the verdict — so the feeling gets managed for the parent's sake rather than the child's.

  - mirrors → Under-Identification With The Child (https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242)
  - contrasts_with → Separation Between Parent And Child (https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242)
  - source: Early Experiences Of The Secure Attachment Style @242s — https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242

### Sensitive Parenting
*origin · literature · secure=secure-form*

The caregiving that produces security, and she is emphatic it is not perfect caregiving. It is emotional attunement plus the capacity to repair after a rupture — which means securely attaching parents are the ones you hear apologising most, not least.

  - mirrors → Inconsistent Responsiveness (https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=121)
  - mirrors → Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility (https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=121)
  - source: Early Experiences Of The Secure Attachment Style @242s — https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242

### Subtle Discomfort At Negative Emotion
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

No cruelty and no hitting — a parent who was themselves taught to suppress, and who becomes slightly stressed or faintly contemptuous when the child shows something negative. The child reads the difference in warmth precisely and concludes, without any of this reaching words, that cheerfulness is what buys access.

  - mirrors → Misattuned Mirroring (https://youtu.be/4avJofwpVNw?t=300)
  - contrasts_with → Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility (https://youtu.be/4avJofwpVNw?t=460)
  - source: Anxious vs Avoidant Attachment Styles & Emotional Pain @300s — https://youtu.be/4avJofwpVNw?t=300

### The Family Scapegoat Role
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

The child who breaks the unspoken rule that the family's dysfunction is not discussed, and is called crazy, irrational or over-reacting for it. Priebe suspects this background sits behind most fearful-avoidant development: a healthy response to injustice gets pathologised until the child concludes that any anger it feels is evidence of its own malfunction.

  - mirrors → Attachment-Seeking Met With Hostility (https://youtu.be/QFrkbdUIYFM?t=200)
  - source: How The Fearful-Avoidant Attachment Style Deals With Anger @200s — https://youtu.be/QFrkbdUIYFM?t=200

### The Trauma Of What Didn't Happen
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

The absence Priebe says gets missed most often — people recognise themselves in the symptoms and can point to nothing in their childhood that was overtly traumatic. What did not happen was being taught to make sense of the relationship between an inner world and an outer one. Research links a subset of depression, anxiety, complex trauma, addiction, insecure attachment and dysregulation back to it.

  - mirrors → Misattuned Mirroring (https://youtu.be/lsBPvgnCJsQ?t=120)
  - contrasts_with → Sensitive Parenting (https://youtu.be/lsBPvgnCJsQ?t=380)
  - source: Emotional Neglect: Healing From The Hidden Trauma Of What Didn't Happen @120s — https://youtu.be/lsBPvgnCJsQ?t=120

### Under-Identification With The Child
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core fearful-avoidant=alternating*

The other failure mode: practical provision treated as the whole of the job, with warmth and responsiveness not counted as needs at all. Nothing bad has happened, so the child is left to manage the feeling alone — which is precisely the lesson that gets learned.

  - contrasts_with → Separation Between Parent And Child (https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242)
  - source: Early Experiences Of The Secure Attachment Style @242s — https://youtu.be/9mOGpwcAfKk?t=242

### Unprocessable Emotion In The Caregiver
*origin · priebe · dismissive-avoidant=core anxious-preoccupied=core fearful-avoidant=core secure=secondary*

Why insecure attachment runs in families without anyone intending it. A parent can only teach a child to metabolise the emotions they can metabolise themselves; the ones they cannot get quietly rejected, often by a parent convinced they are being fully available. Her example is a parent whose own shame fires whenever their child gets angry.

  - source: How Does An Anxious Attachment Style Develop? @188s — https://youtu.be/EdpaCMW1PHw?t=188

### Withheld Information
*origin · literature · dismissive-avoidant=alternating anxious-preoccupied=alternating fearful-avoidant=core*

Growing up without access to the information needed to make sense of what is happening. Her worked example is a parent displacing rage about a spouse's affair onto the child who resembles them: the punishment is real and its actual cause is hidden, so neither reasoning nor feeling ever becomes a reliable predictor.

  - source: How Does A Fearful-Avoidant Attachment Style Develop? @1065s — https://youtu.be/_gCOo_vQM54?t=1065

## style

### Anxious-Preoccupied
*style · literature*

## Does this sound like you?

You know when something has shifted before anyone says so. A change in tone, a slower reply, a slightly different goodbye — you notice, and then you cannot stop noticing.

You are willing to work at a relationship, and you may find that the working never quite ends. You say you want someone consistent and available, and you may notice you have not often chosen one. When a strong feeling arrives, the route back to feeling alright generally runs through another person.

This is not neediness, and it is not too much. It is what a system learns when care arrived reliably enough to be worth reaching for, and unpredictably enough that reaching had to be loud.

> [!tip] You can be different in different relationships
> These are descriptions of what a system does under stress, not personality types. People run differently with different people and at different times, and the point of reading one is recognition, not classification.

### Dismissive-Avoidant
*style · literature*

## Does this sound like you?

You would say you want a long-term relationship and mean it. What tends to happen is that someone you were genuinely interested in stops landing, without an event that explains it — and it arrives feeling like clarity, like you have finally seen them properly.

You solve your own problems. You are good in a crisis. You may not be able to locate what you feel until it is large, and when you do find something that does not seem warranted, your instinct is to work out why it is mistaken. Other people's visible need can produce something closer to disgust than sympathy.

None of that is a character defect. It is what a system learns when reaching for someone reliably cost more than it returned.

> [!tip] You can be different in different relationships
> These are descriptions of what a system does under stress, not personality types. People run differently with different people and at different times, and the point of reading one is recognition, not classification.

### Fearful-Avoidant
*style · literature*

## Does this sound like you?

You want closeness and you cannot settle into it. The pattern often peaks when things are going well — calm, open, no crisis — because that is the point at which something in you starts waiting for the turn.

You may have left relationships you then wanted back within a fortnight, and been unable to explain either move. You are hard on yourself about it, and the harshness is usually worse than anything the situation warrants.

You did not choose this. It is what a system learns when the person who was the source of safety was also, sometimes, the source of danger — and both readings were correct.

> [!tip] You can be different in different relationships
> These are descriptions of what a system does under stress, not personality types. People run differently with different people and at different times, and the point of reading one is recognition, not classification.

### Secure
*style · literature*

## What this looks like

Not the absence of conflict, and not calmness under fire. Secure attachment mostly looks like taking your own distress seriously early, while there are still options — rather than being unusually composed once it is severe.

Both programs stay online: what you appreciate about someone and what the relationship costs you, at the same time, which is what makes an actual negotiation possible. Feeling and reasoning are both available at once instead of taking turns.

This page is the reference point the other three are moving toward. It is a direction, not a finish line, and nobody is at it all the time.

> [!tip] You can be different in different relationships
> These are descriptions of what a system does under stress, not personality types. People run differently with different people and at different times, and the point of reading one is recognition, not classification.
